title: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time
content:
OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources.
If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.
OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said.
OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses.
But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion. OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users, but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans.
Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude-maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth.
OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks.
OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon, said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October.
(Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.)
None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open-source AI labs, especially those from China.

report.summary: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly topped $10B for the first time, up nearly 50% from Q2, as it pushes enterprise products and agents while losses narrow.
report.background: OpenAI was among the first companies to commercialize large AI models and built a massive consumer base, claiming over a billion users. But much of that audience is on free or low-cost plans, and the company had lagged rival Anthropic in selling to enterprises. Earlier this year, OpenAI’s growth looked strong but less explosive than Anthropic’s. The Claude maker has surged in enterprise AI, reportedly reaching $17B in Q3 revenue and an $81B annual run rate while preparing a major IPO. OpenAI has responded with tighter pricing, discounts, improved models, and more enterprise-focused products and AI agents. The reported $10B quarter suggests that strategy is gaining traction, though competition from Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and low-cost open-source models remains intense.
key_points: OpenAI’s Q3 revenue reportedly crossed $10B, up from $6.7B in Q2—an almost 50% jump. Bloomberg cited anonymous sources, so the figure is unconfirmed. The report also says OpenAI reached a $50B annual revenue run rate, a striking milestone for a company that was growing more slowly earlier in the year.

Profitability improved but remains deeply negative. OpenAI’s adjusted operating margin reportedly narrowed from -150% in Q2 to -109% in Q3. That means the company still spends far more than it earns on an adjusted basis, likely reflecting heavy compute, talent, and infrastructure costs, but the direction is toward less severe losses.

OpenAI is leaning into enterprise sales and AI agents after falling behind Anthropic in business adoption. Tighter pricing, discounts, better models, and task-completing agent products appear to be helping. Anthropic still leads on reported enterprise revenue, with $17B in Q3 and an $81B annual run rate, but OpenAI’s latest numbers show it is not ceding the market.

The competitive field is widening beyond OpenAI and Anthropic. Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google are building rival models and platforms, while open-source labs—especially in China—offer cheaper but capable alternatives. OpenAI’s huge user base helps distribution, but converting free and low-cost users into higher-value enterprise and agent customers is the central monetization challenge.

Revenue comparisons need caveats. OpenAI and Anthropic calculate annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by cloud partners, while OpenAI reports only its share of some partner sales. That makes headline run-rate figures useful but not perfectly apples-to-apples, and the reported OpenAI numbers remain unofficial until the company confirms them.
report.impact: The milestone suggests paid AI demand is still expanding rapidly, even as skeptics question whether AI revenues can justify massive infrastructure spending. For the AI industry, it validates enterprise agents and business-focused AI as the next major battleground, intensifying pressure on Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and open-source providers. For developers, expect more agent tooling, enterprise APIs, and price competition, but also vendor lock-in and shifting terms. For regular users, the push toward monetization may bring more capable workplace assistants and embedded AI features, while free tiers could face limits or upsells. The caveat is profitability: OpenAI’s margin is still deeply negative, so revenue growth alone does not prove the business model is sustainable.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch OpenAI’s API and Agents SDK, Anthropic’s Claude API, and OpenRouter for comparing model access and pricing. For builders, LangChain and LlamaIndex are useful for agent and RAG prototypes, while vLLM supports self-hosted open-source models. These tools help developers test whether enterprise AI agents can deliver value without depending on a single vendor.
